Subject: Throughput / latency mapping for Dedicated capacity (Fjord POC)

Camila / Ben —

Thanks for the conversation last week. To help Fjord size a dedicated pool for our image-to-text summarization inference, we need a concrete mapping from our expected token velocity to GPU slabs and what SLO headroom looks like. High-level profile below:

- Peak sustained tokens/sec (ingress): ~15,000 tokens/sec during business hours (short bursts to 25k for <5 minutes)
- Typical prompt + response average tokens: 900 tokens per request (seq len ~1024)
- Target p95 end-to-end latency: <= 250ms
- Model variant: we plan to use an Llama-2-ish 13B open model with quantization (we can use Redwood-verified quantized variant)
- KV cache behavior: onboarding will have low cache hit initially (~10%), expected to improve to ~60% after warm-up

Can you provide a tokens/sec -> GPUs mapping, recommended headroom for capacity / fault tolerance, and rough committed vs burst pricing options?

Also attaching our sample telemetry (small CSV) separately — procurement is looped for budget. Would like a short call to review the numbers tomorrow if possible.

Alex —

Thanks for the clear profile. I did a rapid sizing pass and attached an editable workbook (fjord_compute_model_v1.xlsx) with the assumptions so you can tweak cache hit, seq len, and burst windows. Summary here (ballpark):

- Baseline serving assumptions (redwood-13b-quant, conservative kernel set):
  - Single A100-80GB equivalent (opt kernels, quantized) => ~3,500 tokens/sec sustained at p95 ~220ms (with continuous batching, 64-token batch target)
  - Cold-start and low-cache penalty: p95 increases by ~35%-50% for first 10–15 minutes of ramp unless prefix caching enabled

- Mapping to your 15k tps sustained:
  - Compute: 15,000 / 3,500 = 4.3 => round up to 5 GPUs for baseline sustained throughput
  - Burst capacity to 25k for up to 5 mins: add 2 GPUs (burst slab) to absorb peak without moving to a lower-tier model
  - Operational headroom / failure tolerance: recommend 2x N+1 buffer across availability zones for Dedicated (i.e., target pool of 10 GPUs to provide headroom and rolling upgrades)

- Latency fit: with the above layout and KV cache warmed, expected p95 ~= 200–240ms. If cache stays cold, expect p95 closer to 300–350ms for a short warm-up window.

Recommendations / next steps:
1) Enable prefix/KV caching early in the pilot to reduce the warm-up penalty (we can pre-warm production KV caches during the canary).
2) Start pilot on 6 GPUs (5 baseline + 1 warm-up headroom) and provision a 2-GPU burst slab for the first month while we observe real burst patterns. After month 1, scale to 10 GPUs for 2x headroom if traffic shapes as forecast.
3) If you want a lower-cost option, we can provide a quantized-8bit variant that increases tokens/sec/GPU by ~20% but will need a quality check.

I attached the workbook with cell-level formulas. Please review and we can run a quick screen share tomorrow.

Attachments: fjord_compute_model_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet), fjord_latency-profiles.pdf (latency profile charts)

Quick technical caveats to call out for the model so expectations align:
- KV cache hit ratio is the dominant lever here. Moving from 10% to 60% hit reduces per-request compute by ~45%. If Fjord can pre-warm frequent prefixes (customer IDs / top prompts), you’ll see effective tokens/sec/GPU jump substantially.
- Batching shape matters: continuous batching with 50–100ms queueing gives the best throughput/latency tradeoff. Avoid aggressive batching delays that add latency to p95 SLA calculations.
- Quantization: 8-bit with per-channel scales is fine for many generative tasks, but with some summarization prompts you may observe subtle quality regressions. Recommend a small eval set (we can run Redwood Optimize) before committing to quant-8 for production.
- Cold-model swap / fallback policy: design routing so a lower-cost model variant can accept overflow at higher latency rather than failing requests when capacity saturated.

If we agree on the pilot (6+2 layout), I’ll draft a short runbook for warm-up, KV prefill, and canary checks. Happy to join the call.

—Karthik
